speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: But not if we can enable our people to learn, unlearn and relearn to stay employable over a longer career span.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Indeed, technology is a potential game changer that can allow us to overcome our resource constraints and embark on a new S curve in our growth trajectory.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To stay competitive, we need to be able to innovate and leverage on technology, to do more with less, and to work smart.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Public Service must be able, agile and adaptable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Able to stay at the forefront of technological advancement, agile to be able to work with the private and people sectors to build a competitive economy; and adaptable, as we embrace the journey towards being a Smart Nation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This means that the Public Service must be able to use technology to become more productive in its operations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This includes using technology to transform the way it delivers services.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Citizens today are used to services like FoodPanda or Grab that crowdsource and bring different providers together to be accessible at the fingertips of customers in a high-tech way.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Many companies, such as those in the retail sector, are also using artificial intelligence (AI) and data analytics to analyse and, in fact, anticipate customers' needs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: How is the public sector using technology to similarly transform the way it functions – from performing regulatory functions to enforcement, to delivering services to citizens?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: How can it bring related services together to help citizens or businesses, rather than have citizens or businesses go to different Government agencies to get what they need?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: How is the Public Service using technology to make service delivery more efficient and save time and effort on the part of citizens and businesses in transacting with the public sector?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In fact, how is the Public Service using AI and data analytics to better anticipate citizens' needs and using robotics to complement its workforce?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Of course, it is not and must not be just a tech push.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Ultimately, Public Service delivery must be anchored on citizens' needs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Beyond delivering services efficiently and impartially, the Public Service must be able to put in place systems and processes to ensure that public officers do not just apply rules mechanically but always put citizens at the heart of Public Service delivery.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: They must be able to identify changes in the needs of citizens and be able to update policies, programmes and services in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In short, the three "highs": not just high-tech but also high touch; and not just high touch but also high trust.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To transform public services, therefore, requires public officers to take on new skills so that they can perform their jobs differently and effectively.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Where work can be automated, it is also important for public officers to be able to take on new skills to perform new jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Does the Public Service put in place reskilling programmes to help retrain officers to move from one job to another within the public sector as technology changes the way work is done?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Public Service should work closely with our public sector unions and the Labour Movement to encourage all officers to constantly reskill and retool in order to keep themselves relevant and employable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: A good start will be forming dedicated training committees jointly with our public sector unions and union leaders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Beyond skills, the Public Service ethos lies at the heart of Public Service.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While jobs and skills will change, the values of service, integrity and excellence should always remain.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: How is the Public Service developing its officers to ensure that they continue to remain grounded, that they are in touch rather than lose touch with the needs, aspirations and concerns of citizens and businesses?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: How do we develop public officers who are able to serve with heart, be able to connect with citizens and co-create new solutions with both the people and private sectors?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore has one of the most dynamic and high performance public service sector globally.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: With a spectrum of younger officers to the very senior and experienced ones, they serve Singaporeans through our Ministries, Civil Service, Statutory Boards and many other organisations.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: With globalisation and a more connected world, our Public Service must be resourceful, creative and rapid thinking.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They must remain nimble and keep abreast of the changes and disruption in the world of today and tomorrow.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They must align with the state of the art, be adaptable and flexible in certain aspects of policymaking and governance, but yet uphold the principles that Singapore stands for.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The adoption of information technology (IT) and other technology-driven processes, communications as well as surveillance must be top-notch and robust.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Yet at the same time, maintenance of safety and security must be upheld.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And this is also part of the learn, unlearn and relearn process.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Another very important tagline with the Public Service must be coordination.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Mr Chairman, my cut today is to discuss whether our Public Service can adopt a citizen-centric approach to delivering Government services.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Delivering services to citizens is at the core of what Government agencies do.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Unfortunately, many of these services are based on processes and technologies that have been in place for many years and many of these were designed based on each agency's individual needs and requirements.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Therefore, such services were not designed with the objective of improving the ease and satisfaction when a citizen interacts or transacts with the Government.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: To make an enquiry or to complete a transaction, citizens may have to physically visit different agencies, speak on the phone with multiple parties or browse the websites of various Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Often times, citizens have to fill up many forms and repeat information that were previously provided albeit to a different Government department.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Today, with advances in technology and connectivity, Governments can meet these rising citizen expectations.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Digital transformation with AI, machine-learning and data analytics, a Government could even predict and anticipate what a citizen needs.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Queuing at counters and filling up forms could be a thing of the past.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Trust, as they say, is built in drops and lost in buckets.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The recent spate of service lapses has contributed to an increasing sense of uncertainty about the robustness of the Public Service.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat, in response to the Zaobao commentary that alleged complacency, said "We would not flinch from taking a hard look at ourselves each time there is a failure and doing whatever is necessary to put things right." I am heartened by Minister Heng's conviction and commitment.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, a string of events of such significance happening so fast and furiously offers more than a glimpse of possible fault lines within the system, not just in isolated Ministries or with certain officers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Might having an open conversation on these fault lines restore trust?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, how does the Public Service Division (PSD) ensure a culture of accountability, transparency and empathy?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: With increased public scrutiny and expectations, how is the Civil Service College (CSC) training public officers to understand subjective well-being beyond material well-being and how are they trained to formulate better policies that address citizens' well-being in ways that also increase public trust in public institutions?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, how can Public Service Cares, announced in Budget 2019, be more than just a volunteering programme for public officers, but be embodied as an ethos?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It often contains embarrassing findings and may uncover misconduct.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The AGO reports are a key measure by the Government towards accountability and the prudent use of public funds.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, today, I would like to ask for clarification about the selection process and criteria used by the Prime Minister in selecting the Auditor-General.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Constitution does not spell out any qualifying criteria for being the Auditor-General.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In recent history, our Auditor-Generals have been drawn from senior civil servants and there has been an appointment of a new Auditor-General this year.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I do not know the current appointee personally and I have no reason to doubt her integrity.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: As I understood from some pensioners, they have continued to receive the same medical benefit as before, as assured in this House, although not under MediShield Life but under their original pension medical scheme.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: As it is, these pensioners are insured under MediShield Life in name only even though they do not need the coverage.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I understand their MediShield Life premiums are paid for by the Government and transitional subsidies through MediSave top-ups.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The MediShield Life scheme is almost five years now.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: While pensioners are not worse off, in terms of their medical benefits, I wish to ask the Government if there is any study or survey done to ascertain the financial impact of the redundant MediShield Life coverage on pensioners.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: After factoring in the various MediSave top-ups, did the subsidies help pensioners pay for their MediShield Life premiums as well as for their spouses' premium in full without the need to incur any out-of-pocket expenses?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This is important because this Government has assured pensioners in this House that they would not be worse off under MediShield Life.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: By that, it should also mean that they would not be financially burdened when they are put under the compulsory but never used medical scheme.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Next, Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean said that pensioners have one important benefit with MediShield Life that they did not have previously.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: He said that the spouse of a pensioner will cease to have medical benefits when the pensioner passes away.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But under MediShield Life, the spouse will be covered by MediShield when the pensioner is no longer around.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Everyone has to pay for medical coverage by law, regardless of who you are.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, this important MediShield Life benefit, as mentioned by the Minister, only makes more sense for pensioners if the Government continues to pay the premium for their spouses when they are no longer around.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Otherwise, the spouses will have to come under MediShield Life by law as they do not have a choice.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, in Prime Minister Lee's "A Tale of Two Cities" speech in London in 2014, he espoused Singapore's global city aspirations.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: To this end, we achieved 5th place in the Global Cities Outlook List last year.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: To sustain this, it is imperative that our world-class city is supported by a world-class Civil Service.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In addition, I would like to suggest that the Government use the speed of delivery and the quality of Public Services as metrics by which it assesses the progress of its push to build a world-class Civil Service.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, it should be noted that the employment of a one-size-fits-all approach in serving the public will not suffice.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: There must be greater introspection on the part of our Civil Service.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Far too often, we focus too much on the numbers and neglect the human aspect of governance.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: While automation has allowed for gains in productivity, navigating a pre-recorded voice menu or filling up a form adhering to a strict format online, may not satisfy the needs of the public.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the pursuit of headcount and productivity key performance indicators (KPIs), the public sector has resorted to outsourcing, which has affected the quality of public services.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: At the same time, we should refocus our efforts to train and deepen the skills of our Public Service officers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, the Government has been active in its efforts to innovate and improve the ease of transactions between the Government and the public.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the pace of transformation quickens with technological disruptions, I would like to know how well public sector workers are being prepared to stay relevant.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, how have jobs in the public sector been transformed and what other changes will be coming soon?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the midst of such changes, I hope the Government can take the lead in ensuring that all public sector workers have access to relevant training, reskilling and redeployment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are the various Ministries and agencies aware of the challenges faced by those who may struggle in their training efforts, especially the older workers, who may find it more challenging to acquire new skillsets?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Have we been able to redeploy these workers across different departments, agencies or Ministries?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Recently, I met about 80 unionised staff from various Statutory Boards and they shared with me their experiences and the assistance given to help our public sector workers to be future-ready and to be prepared for a transformed workplace.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is PSD aware of how each agency is progressing in this journey and whether their respective efforts have been effective, especially to help the older ones adjust to the pace of training required for their new or enhanced job roles or even redeployed roles?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry have an update on the take-up rate of these courses on the new learning portal?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung shared that one initiative was to merge existing schemes for diploma and degree holders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister provide an update on which other public agencies no longer have different salary scales and progression structures for diploma and degree holders?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can we also extend this to the Institute of Technical Education (ITE) graduates and not just diploma and degree holders?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, we need to close the feedback loop so that public servants know that their views are valued and can make a difference in strengthening the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I suggested implementing internal QSMs within Ministries and Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung responded that all public agencies do conduct staff engagement surveys periodically.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I still meet some public servants who say that they have provided feedback but have no idea if anyone is looking into it and have not received the reply with regard to the feedback that was provided.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Minister consider adopting common principles and guidelines for the conduct of staff engagement surveys across the Public Service?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Minister also consider requiring public agencies to track the feedback received and actions taken in response to the feedback?

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, let me first thank all Members who have spoken up in support of the importance of maintaining an able and committed Public Service.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our Public Service colleagues and I are determined to build a Public Service that is the pride of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our Public Service has been a pillar of strength for Singapore's survival and success.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It has been so, and it will continue to be so.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Internally, new generations of Singaporeans are growing up in different circumstances, with different aspirations and expectations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Singaporeans expect services to be organised around them and delivered in an integrated and timely manner.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They expect systems and organisations to fit their needs and not the other way round.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Singaporeans also expect services and information at their fingertips and have much less patience to navigate complex bureaucracies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Externally, our geopolitical situation has become more uncertain and challenging.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: New security threats, including the cyberspace, have emerged and which threaten our national security.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The contest of big powers and the domestic politics of regional players combined, can potentially squeeze us and shrink our economic and foreign policy options.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Connectivity and technology allow us the opportunities to overcome our geographical and labour constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If used well, they can bring us to greater heights.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our workforce is also more educated and more skilled.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We can better compete on quality rather than quantity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To continue to build a vibrant and successful Singapore for the future, our Public Service must constantly challenge ourselves to come up with new ideas, adopt fresh approaches to working, organise ourselves differently and develop new skills.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our Public Service generally delivers services efficiently, but this is not enough.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Beyond working the whole-of-Government, our Public Service must achieve whole-of-Nation outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Partnering Singaporeans and the private sector to deliver results must become second nature to our Public Service, and not as an afterthought.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is not just about delivering good service for the public but also delivering better services with the public.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: However, the Public Service and private sector must play our respective parts well in this new partnership to take Singapore to greater heights.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Both must be mature to know the complexities of taking into account many sources of feedback, competing interests and differing aspirations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And if our individual suggestion is not accepted after working the process together, it does not mean that the ideas and inputs are not considered.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Instead, it has formed part of the process to arrive at the final solution.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I agree with Dr Teo Ho Pin on a design-thinking approach to the delivery of public services.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The team wanted to make life easier for parents of newborn babies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They want to reduce the administrative hassle so that mums and dads can focus on welcoming baby and caring for baby.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, they started by interviewing many new parents to understand what needs to be done at the point of baby’s birth, what frustrates them and to get good ideas from parents how public services can be delivered better and faster services for them.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will also design services with different segments of citizens in mind, especially those who may not find it easy to access our services through the usual channels.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For instance, at the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS), a priority registration queue is created for the elderly and those with mobility constraints during the tax filing season.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They will be ushered to a sitting area and attended to quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Housing and Development Board (HDB) also sets up a priority queue during sales launches to assist the elderly, persons with disabilities and expectant mothers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: At the Central Provident Fund (CPF) Board's service centres, there are retired citizens who serve as roving CPF Ambassadors to help post-55 CPF members.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Public Service is working closely with various people and private sector organisations in this expanded effort to redesign services around citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will share more about these developments in the coming months.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Within the Public Service, we also need to organise work differently across Ministries and agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our current structures were optimised to solve previous problems.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: When problems evolved and goals changed, we must similarly be bold to evolve our structures and organisations to serve the objectives of tomorrow, as Member Mr Cedric Foo suggested.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Climate change, cyber threats, unmanned systems are but some new challenges that require us to evolve new organisational structures to manage them.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Cedric Foo also asked how we can continue to ensure that our services are citizen-centric.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Indeed, the Public Service must reorganise itself to be citizen-centric, not agency-centric, in the way we work.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Public Service Centre at Our Tampines Hub is one example.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Citizens will be able to approach any counter for help, instead of having to wait for the "right" counter to become available.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Social Service Office (SSO) is yet another example of how we are bringing different services together to help citizens in need.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Silver Generation Office (SGO) is also co-located with the SSOs in Taman Jurong and Geylang Serai, and the officers work closely to address the social and health needs of seniors in a more integrated manner.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As many have suggested, it is not easy for the Public Service to organise itself differently and operate differently to serve citizens better without new skills.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Ms Anthea Ong, Dr Teo Ho Pin and Mr Ang Hin Kee are right that we have to help our public officers approach their work with new mindsets and give them new skills.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, we need our public officers to think differently.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They must be able to see beyond the current task that they are doing, and work with their colleagues in other Ministries or agencies to serve citizens better.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This does not come from classroom training alone.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: PSD will expand the system of job postings to apply to a wider group of officers, so that our officers will gain wider perspectives, and grow a stronger instinct to work across agencies and with the private and people sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second, our public officers cannot just develop good policies but must be able to execute them well.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To do this, public officers must be able to understand the needs of citizens and businesses better, know what are the constraints and challenges on the ground in implementing policies, and be able to see through the implementation details.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Leaders at Director-level and above were attached to different frontline work environments to serve citizens so that they can gain new insights on how policies and programmes can be implemented better on the ground.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This year, we will implement Public Service Cares.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is a new initiative to encourage all officers to volunteer and serve the community and, in the process, learn how to better communicate with citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It seeks to develop a stronger service ethos and a culture among public servants to walk and know the ground needs even better.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Officers, senior ones including, are regularly rotated to join the People's Association (PA), SSOs and the feedback unit Reaching Everyone for Active Citizenry @ Home (REACH) outreach efforts on the ground for them to get a first-hand feel of serving Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Third, we need our public officers to have good interpersonal linkages with the people and private sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In particular, the Public Service will work towards achieving greater porosity and two-way flow of talents between the public and the people and private sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: One way is through sending officers to work attachments in the private sector.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They are bringing back new knowledge and insights to improve the delivery of public services.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will expand such opportunities to strengthen our Public Service and our links beyond the Public Service.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Fourth, public officers need to understand our region much better and develop stronger ties with their peers in the region.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To continue to expand the economic and international space for Singapore, our officers must be able to be plugged into various international networks and understand the economic, political and social systems of countries in the region and in our key markets.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our Public Service leadership must be able to pick up a phone and call their peers to discuss issues and to engage in new collaboration.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Therefore, we will continue to encourage both Public Service Commission (PSC) scholars as well as mid-career officers to be trained in different countries.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will also create many more opportunities for officials across different countries to come together in joint courses, forums and discussions to share best practices and network together.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Just as in the private sector, we should expect future Public Service leaders to have experiences working beyond the domestic context.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Every public officer, from leaders to counter staff, must know how to operate in a digital world and to thrive in it.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The CSC has launched LEARN, a mobile platform to enable officers to learn anytime, anywhere.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Smart Nation and Digital Government Office (SNDGO) will elaborate more on other Smart Nation Initiatives subsequently.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I agree with several Members who spoke on the need to create a more diverse Public Service leadership.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We need a Public Service leadership team that has different talents and is able to surface different perspectives.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: A more diverse Public Service is a more resilient Public Service for the uncertainties ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must systematically select, recruit and develop officers to achieve this diversity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Educational qualifications remain a valid proxy for certain skills and capabilities of candidates we recruit into the Public Service, and we will not disregard that.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But the level of educational qualification alone is necessary but not sufficient.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Public Service will also have to look out for other skills, competencies and traits when we recruit new officers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Beyond intellect, we also want officers who have initiative and creative ideas, and those who have strong interpersonal skills and work well with others.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In the areas of information and communications technology (ICT), the Public Service will be selecting recruits based on the technical skills they possess, beyond educational qualifications.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about single structures for ITE graduates, diploma and degree holders.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Where schemes require particular qualifications, for example, doctors, accountants and engineers, we will specify these.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Today, almost all public agencies have single structure schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I have spoken at length about how the Public Service needs to change.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But just as important are things that will not change: our values, our aspirations for Singapore and the high standards for ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our values of excellence mean that we will not rest on our laurels.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our Public Service continues to work towards high aspirations for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This means always thinking ahead and acting to expand opportunities for Singapore or pre-empting problems in future.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For instance, for Singapore to remain competitive, we must be a hub for innovation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So, MOE, Enterprise Singapore (ESG) and the Economic Development Board (EDB) came together to develop the Global Innovation Alliance (GIA) initiative to connect Singapore to major innovation ecosystems around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The GIA expands on existing overseas internship programmes offered by our local institutes of higher education that place students on overseas internships in startups or enterprising and innovative companies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Public Service is leveraging these internships for scholarship holders and in-service officers as well for them to broaden their training and exposure.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: GIA will create more opportunities for students, entrepreneurs and business owners to gain experience, connect and collaborate with their overseas counterparts.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Similarly, we have proactively pushed for more Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) to help our businesses expand overseas and lower prices of imported goods and services for domestic consumers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Such FTAs have to be planned way ahead, as they entail long negotiations with foreign counterparts.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They worked together and sustained the momentum of the negotiations through time across different teams of officers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are now planning ahead for our FTAs to embrace digital trade in the new economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We also think long term when it comes to developing our city.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Almost 10 years ago, the Economic Strategies Committee mooted the idea of consolidating our container port activities at Tuas in the long term.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This will allow our port to achieve greater economies of scale while freeing up the prime Southern Waterfront for redevelopment into a new waterfront city that will be even more exciting than Marina Bay.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Tuas Terminal, which will be twice the size of Ang Mo Kio town, is expected to be the largest container terminal in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our Tuas Terminal will help Singapore strengthen our position in the maritime sector.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is not the only long-term multi-decade projects we have planned for.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are pursuing other ambitious projects that span many years, in fact, decades, whether it is developing Singapore's deepest cable tunnel system for electricity transmission or planning for Changi East which includes the new Terminal 5, or planning for the Jurong Innovation District or Punggol Digital District.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These projects help to create an even more vibrant Singapore and a better home for future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our Public Service cannot just try to play defensive to uphold the existing system.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We expect more from our Public Service constantly thinking of breaking new ground to take the country forward amidst the stiff competition.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Even though we plan ahead, sometimes things will not go as planned.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: When things do go wrong, the Public Service will work hard to fix the mistakes and seek to do better.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Head (Civil Service) recently reminded all senior public leaders to use the recent incidents and lapses as an important learning moment to see how we can do better.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I support his call and appreciate that the Public Service is taking its mission very seriously.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: However, integrity means that we need to take responsibility and be accountable at every level for what went wrong.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If we do not address the mistake head-on at the respective levels, but instead choose to indiscriminately sack staff and leaders every time something went wrong, then we will have a weaker system over time.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will also discourage the Public Service from trying new things because the surest way not to make a mistake, is not to do anything novel.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: That will be the biggest mistake and disservice to our nation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The values of integrity and excellence apply equally to the appointment processes.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The process to appoint individuals to any constitutional appointments is set out in the Constitution.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Constitution also sets out the requirements of candidates for certain roles, as well as the officeholders who should be advised or to be consulted on the appointment.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In general, the key considerations when identifying candidates include their ability to do the job well, their qualifications and experience, track record, integrity and sense of Public Service.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The President will consult the Council of Presidential Advisors which provides an additional level of scrutiny and advice.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Ms Goh Soon Poh has more than 30 years of public sector experience and worked in a range of Government Ministries.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: She has served with distinction, with utmost integrity and commitment to excellence.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: She has helmed Deputy Secretary roles in two of the largest Ministries, MOE and the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), and also spent time in two central Ministries, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) and PSD, and will be familiar with governance matters related to finance, procurement and human resources.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Ms Goh Soon Poh also has public sector experience that will be useful for the Auditor-General role.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The role of the Auditor-General is to audit and report to the President and Parliament on the proper accounting and use of public resources to enhance public accountability.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: AGO's audit observations are conveyed to senior public officers, namely, Permanent Secretaries of Ministries who are Accounting Officers for their respective Ministries and, hence, responsible for managing that.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These senior public officers are responsible for addressing the findings and reporting back to the AGO.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The audit process generally does not involve political officeholders.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There is no conflict of interest generally between AGO and the Ministries it audits.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Where there is a potential conflict of interest, there are specific processes to manage these, just as in any professional organisation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: PSD currently works with Public Sector agencies to administer a common staff engagement survey across public agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The survey enables agency leaders to better understand the areas that the agency is doing well in and what it can do better to help officers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Leaders are expected to respond to the feedback and take appropriate action.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Png Eng Huat asked about MediShield Life for pensioners.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: MediShield Life provides additional help on top of the retirement medical benefits that they enjoy as Government pensioners.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is very useful, especially if someone is unfortunate enough to get a severe illness with a huge medical bill.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For example, one pensioner on the Comprehensive Co-payment Scheme (CCS) had pneumonia with a bill size of $29,000.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: She had 85% of the bill covered by her post-retirement medical benefits.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: MediShield Life helped to pay for the remaining 15%.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: She did not have to pay anything out of pocket.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Another pensioner on the CCS had lymphoma with a bill size of about $14,000.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: He only had to pay out-of-pocket expenses of $300, after taking into account his post-retirement medical benefits and MediShield Life.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, our public officers joined our Public Service because of a calling.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And that is to build a better home, a better nation and a better future for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our future is in the hands of this generation of leaders – from the public, private and the people sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Like it was almost 54 years ago, we must all be pioneers once more and always.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In fact, this is a global trend among developed and developing economies around the world, and it will certainly take time to find sustainable solutions to alleviate the situation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: That a woman should have a career and also be a good mother; that a man should have a career and also be a good father.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We give them good support with maternity leave, paternity leave, childcare leave, Baby Bonus and a whole suite of incentives.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Difficulty in juggling office work and care for children, from tending to them when they are sick, to coaching them as they grow up.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This will also foster strong family ties and give our children a strong foundation, too.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We can make laws where these women and men would not be discriminated against for the years out of the job market.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In return, we can allow more qualified older people in our workforce to stay on to fill the vacant slots temporarily left behind by them.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As we continue to implement baby-friendly policies as well as family-friendly policies, we must continue to identify and manage other problems stemming from an ageing population.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We are encouraging senior citizens to stay healthy and active in the workforce through a lot of initiatives.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Perhaps we can incentivise our senior citizens to look after their grandchildren.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We face greater challenges with our limited pool of human resources to maintain a vibrant economy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How has the Government directed its population strategies to support an economy that will continue to grow?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We rank 13 among countries best at attracting, developing and retaining talent in 2018, according to a report by Business Insider.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If we cannot sustain our population by Singaporeans' natural births, then the only way to top up our population is through immigration.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We will then face the issue of integration and challenges in forging a national identity and cohesion.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As a young nation, we continue to grapple with seeking our national identity.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We do not have a shared history of struggles that binds us together.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Our PG and MG can share their experience and be a valued resource to inspire the next.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Perhaps, the Government can share its plans to foster a strong sense of national identity among Singaporeans, and yet maintain a healthy population profile.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, take the two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A rapidly ageing population and a persistently low Total Fertility Rate (TFR), which is among the lowest in the world, pose serious challenges for our future.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are severe implications for our social fabric, national heritage, economy and defence, just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must make it a matter of priority and urgency to review our population strategies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need a core group of young Singaporeans to ensure that our country remains cohesive, dynamic and vibrant.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What measures does the Government have to invigorate our population strategies and keep a balanced mix of locals and immigrants?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is the Ministry’s view on the effect of new attitudes to family structures and their impact on families and procreation?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, how would we prevent the financial burden of caring for our ageing population from falling on our future generations?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Minister Heng Swee Keat's Budget speech, he urged us to draw on our Singaporean DNA to continue to progress.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Modern Singapore had started as an immigrant country and will continue to accept and integrate immigrants in the future.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, it is important that we have a core group of Singaporeans born and bred here.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government had implemented various measures and incentives to support marriage and procreation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need an urgent review to understand why they have not been effective.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Whether these are inadequate or require enhancements, we must address the roots of the problems.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry share its plans to reverse our TFR?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Immigration laws vary from country to country and change according to the needs, factors affecting population as well as growth and development of the nation.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Singapore is challenged even further due to our sheer small size, and more so due to our rapidly ageing populace.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Our guidelines and policies must acknowledge our diversity, uphold unity and be realistic and practical.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: New citizens can have a positive contribution towards nation-building and social integration.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: The guidelines for recruiting new citizens must be robust and dynamic and at the same time meet our objectives.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Are we able to implement a more structured community involvement of potential new citizen candidates, perhaps even with the provision of inputs from senior and experienced community leaders?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: This is with a view to having them immersed and better integrated in the local community and activities.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: The community leaders can act as assenters and provide valuable inputs in this respect.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is despite the fact that the Government has put in place a wide variety of incentives for people to marry and have children.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: According to Singapore's population data bureau, we have a large number of people of childbearing age and coming to childbearing age, yet more are choosing not to get married and have children.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Have any studies been done on why this is so?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I understand from previous COS debates that many young people have a desire to settle down and get married.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Yet, it appears they are not doing so.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What are the challenges faced, particularly by young adults, in marriage and parenthood?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Is there anything that may be done to address these challenges?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, as a nation, we strive to be the best.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But, sometimes, we have to take a cold hard look at ourselves to take stock.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are a city in a garden, but are we truly green?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are fast becoming a Smart Nation, but can this nation also continue to grow a heart?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have a highly productive workforce, but what are we truly producing?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We can be No 1 on many fronts, but if we allow our most basic of building blocks to start to crumble and weaken, how long more can we keep it up?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Chairman, as Singapore continues to progress economically, it also seems that, like the rest of the developed world, we are beginning to face what is an increasingly post-familist future, one where that basic building block, the family, is becoming more sidelined and threatened.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singlehood, childlessness and instability of the institution of the family are growing in many countries around the world and Singapore has not been spared.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And while not in the extreme, some anti-natalist propaganda has also recently appeared on our shores.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Perhaps it is opportune for us to ask ourselves again what is it that we are not doing enough of?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What I feel is missing from the narrative is addressing the slow unfortunate change in culture and its threat to the family.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We can always admit that – one whose pace is breakneck.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We all want to work hard, produce better results and aim for the next rung up in our careers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But it has unfortunately become a key part of our new culture today.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This work ethic subconsciously makes us stay longer in the office and often even when there is no real reason to do so.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Great for the companies, but at what cost to society?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We end up having no time to date, no time to go out, no time for ourselves, no time to get married, no time to have children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We cannot be indifferent to this problem as a society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our very fabric as a nation depends of the family nucleus.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Families play a vital role in determining the welfare of children, in meeting our deepest needs for meaning and solidarity with one another, and in shaping the economic and political fortunes of nations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When the family is not flourishing and no longer serves as the central organising feature of society, the nation begins to lose its basic unit.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, it is not just about the money.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The more money we throw at the problem, the more monetised and mercantile this most natural of building blocks becomes, reinforcing the growing stereotype that families are commodities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What we need to do today is to reinforce a culture that is centred around the family.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: From our very childhood, we should imbue in our young the importance of family, encouraging them to have quality time with their own families.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For parents of this generation to reset the pace and reset the tempo of our culture.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Part of it is our auto-reverential culture caused by technology.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many of us can attest to the fact that when we are at home, we may be with one another but we are really not with one another, we are with your phones.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We pretend to engage with one another, but actually we ignore one another.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We think we speak to many people but, actually, we are just talking to ourselves.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On the work front, this happens as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Technology meant to make work easier, literally ties us to our desk, even if we are away from the office.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, employers must also see more and more the importance that family plays in having a happy workforce.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: More can be done at the cultural level.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For all the generosity of our Marriage and Parenthood Package, there must also be whole-of-society issues that need to be addressed like cost of living and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How can we ensure that, as a society, we continue to value the family and will be willing to help families achieve their aspirations?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These take more than just policy, programmes or grants, but the whole society and a relook of our culture.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must do what we can to avoid what some called the "systematic humiliation, apathy-inducing neglect and soul-killing cruelty" against the role of families in our society.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Couples these days have many valid concerns when planning to embark on parenthood.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But the broader society, encompassing community groups, employers and families, can do more to compromise and embrace a family-friendly Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are couples who are perfectly happy juggling four children.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are the ones with good support from the community, their extended families and their workplace.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They probably made some personal sacrifices to prioritise their family as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today's grandparents are not like those of the 1960s and 1970s.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today's grandparents plan their retirement and go on frequent holidays, and I do not fault them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, how do we balance between the needs of the grandparents and their young children who are setting up families?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is being done to help instil a family-friendly culture in Singapore which is supportive of marriage and parenthood?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need a mindset shift in our approach to address the issues in this environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many a time, my wife and I, who are both working and have three kids, will face emergency calls from the school or kids falling ill, among other things, requiring one or both of us to attend to a child.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One example of how we can further improve a family culture environment is to see if we can offer some comprehensive back-up care in corporates or private and public agencies with a national software matching platform to help employees find last-minute childcare or eldercare when the usual arrangements breakdown.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the United Kingdom (UK), there are such companies doing it, such as My FamilyCare.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But more can be done to create these private set-ups and help these types of companies grow to create a better and more diverse support network in a family-friendly environment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A man came home and saw his helper at the playground with his children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They were having so much fun and he was jealous.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It had been a long day at work and, at that moment, he felt like he was working so hard so that he could pay his domestic helper to have the life that he wants.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It was a fleeting thought, but it reflected on how much he wished he could spend more time with his children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We all have aspirations and we want a better life for our families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We also have much to contribute to the economy and a meaningful job gives us a sense of purpose and drive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, many of us also yearn for a work-life balance so we can spend time with our families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Employers play an important role in supporting Singaporeans in managing their work-life balance, including providing flexible work arrangements (FWAs) or supporting working fathers in playing more active roles at home.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: How will the Government encourage employers to play their part?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note there are schemes, such as the Enhanced Work-Life Grant.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Have the measures been effective and what more could be done to encourage employers to foster a more family-friendly workplace culture?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our young Singaporeans are sandwiched in caring for young children and elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Government has been providing support to such families.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister update on further progress and what more will the Ministry be doing?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Demographic trends necessitate changes to how young families are supported at the workplaces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: One, with smaller family sizes, our younger Singaporeans need to care for both their children and parents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is common to easily spend more than a day away from work to bring an older parent for medical check-up.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Thus, Family Care Leave is important to our workers, especially those whose children are older than seven.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The fungibility in using the leave provides more flexibility for workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, we need to help our young Singaporean parents better manage the cost of infant care and full-day childcare.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While many companies today offer FWAs, it has not been socialised into a societal norm like the Nordic countries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to take decisive action to make FWA pervasive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This makes starting FWA conversations easier for workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This can provide real impetus in socialising FWA and better support our families, especially our women workers.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It is now not just "money not enough", but also "time and leave not enough".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It does not make sense that the amount of leave does not increase as well when you have more kids.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Parents with four kids clearly need more leave than parents with one child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: With Hand Foot and Mouth Disease (HFMD) so common now, six days of childcare leave are just not enough.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I experienced this last year when all three of my kids had HFMD consecutively.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: My four-year-old had to be out of school for two weeks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am not even sure if parents who have two or more kids will have sufficient annual leave once their childcare leave has been used.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Parents can provide their child's medical certificate (MC) as proof when using this leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In the blink of an eye, my twins, Katie and Poppy, are now two years old.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: From fighting for their lives, they are now fighting for their toys.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Their crying has been replaced by smiles and the beautiful sound of laughter.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This parenthood journey has been priceless, and I am so happy we have three healthy, happy girls.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The Adjournment Motion speech brought back many painful memories of Katie and Poppy being born premature and almost losing their lives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can the Minister confirm if the entire Public Service is now providing this unpaid leave?

speaker: Mr Speaker
