speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In making the point, can I enquire if the EBRC has been formed?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2013, Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean stated that the Prime Minister will certainly remain open to and consider making refinements to its procedures when necessary.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope these suggestions on greater detail in the Committee’s report and announcing when the Committee is formed will be taken on board.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Prime Minister update the House on this matter and the number of roadshows that will be organised for this purpose, where and when they will be held in the months to come?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Committee is made up of senior civil servants who are knowledgeable in demographic shifts and population statistics.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In drawing up its recommendations, the Committee is guided by the terms of reference laid out by the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When reviewing the electoral boundaries, the Committee takes into account technical factors, such as population growth and shifts and other relevant parameters.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As a matter of practice, we should allow the Committee to focus on its work professionally, away from unnecessary media attention or public pressures.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As with past elections, there will be sufficient time, from when the Committee’s review report is made public to the time of the election, for candidates and political parties to make their preparations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And for the number of roadshows, we have done that in preparation for the last Presidential Election and will continue to do that as we move towards the next General Election.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, MAS recently announced a $75 million plan to boost equities research and equity listings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Critics have argued that this is throwing money at the problem without addressing the fundamental issues of stock market malaise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For small to mid-size caps, the main problem seems to be the lack of expertise and experience on corporate governance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even before we can talk about investor excitement, we should address the confidence of retail investors in small and mid-caps.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is often excitement in initial listings, many times encouraged by enthusiastic analyst coverage, but this excitement very easily gives way to collapsing stock prices due to corporate governance issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Recent examples include e-commerce startup Y Ventures and food and beverage (F&B) company Kimly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The restructuring of Noble Group, which has not been allowed to relist, and the current restructuring of Hyflux to save it from liquidation, have further affected confidence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For both Noble and Hyflux, analyst reports have had little impact in educating retail investors about their cash flow problems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Shareholder activism and academic scrutiny have done more to highlight potential issues, but often too late for retail investors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would not the Grant for Equity Market Singapore (GEMS) do better to fund programmes to advise small and mid-caps on corporate governance and improve their performance in this aspect?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, last year, the Keppel Offshore and Marine corruption case was discussed in this House.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many people have wondered how sizeable bribe payments were made without oversight from the highest level of management or its Board.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Like the Swiber case, we are still waiting for the outcome of the Keppel case.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This, in turn, can affect shareholder value and investor confidence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The repercussions of such problems affect many small-scale retail investors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Sixty-year-old Mrs Goh shared with Channel NewsAsia her worries of not being able to recoup her investment in Hyflux.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such worries are not unfounded as recent announcements by Hyflux have indicated that investors like her will have to suffer losses on their investments if a proposed restructuring plan proceeds.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another worry arising from such corporate malfeasance is the impact such incidents can have on the companies' reputation and, by extension, on Singapore’s.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Despite such efforts, it may be time for us to acknowledge that self-regulation and internally-driven processes on corporate governance cannot be relied upon solely.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The present oversight processes and regime are surely not adequate.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In some of these cases, the problems reported seemed to have escaped the attention of their auditors or the problems have not been commented upon by their auditors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In cases where the executive management of a company or its board is aware of serious malfeasance or malpractices or is not aware of such malfeasance but ought to be aware, the buck should never stop anywhere below executive management and its Board.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Regulators should be more proactive in taking errant or neglectful directors to account when they fail in their duties and obligations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can Singapore Exchange Regulation (SGX RegCo) or the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA) not do more?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government should do more to improve the corporate governance regime of our companies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such a review is timely and necessary to ensure that safeguards are in place to protect shareholder value and to ensure that the reputation of Singapore companies is not adversely affected by those who have fallen short.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Mr Chairman, I am heartened that Budget 2019 acknowledges climate change as a strategic challenge for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: The financial sector’s role in allocating capital for a climate-safe future across generations is a significant one that we must include in our strategic plan for climate change action.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: As a leading financial hub, Singapore’s banking and asset management industry must rise to this challenge.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: How we lend is a reflection of our values and principles.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: For example, civil society recently called out our banks for continuing to fund coal-fired power.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: The Governor of the Bank of England is reported to be open to increased regulatory requirements for "brown" investments.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: What regulatory and supervisory mechanisms are being developed so that banks in Singapore will: (a) actively implement existing green standards, like the Association of Banks in Singapore's (ABS’) Haze Diagnostic Kit, into their lending policy frameworks; and (b) proactively work with civil society and experts to identify other critical industries, like energy, where green standards should be developed and implemented?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Can we allocate funds to support our asset management industry to develop stronger stewardship principles and use the tools available in the market to help us safeguard our future, one that is climate-safe?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: For example, the Government Pension Investment Fund of Japan allocates close to 10% of its investments into funds using sustainability indices.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Two pension funds in Korea have gone even further and stepped away from future coal investments.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Chairman, let me first start by addressing Assoc Prof Daniel Goh's question on GEMS.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, it is not funded from taxpayers' money.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The scheme was then designed in response to feedback from the industry that a vibrant equity market requires not only new listings but also sustained investor interest post-listing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, it is really a fund started from the industry to address feedback from the industry and you design GEMS.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And the primary aim is to strengthen public financing channels for growth enterprises, in particular, SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, GEMS does so, as Assoc Prof Goh mentioned, by defraying listing-related expenses and promoting better research coverage of the sectors they are in, as well as their business models.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are certain sectors that we can do better in attracting listings; high growth sectors being one example.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And GEMS is designed to promote those sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are also gaps in investment coverage for small and mid-cap listed enterprises and new business models.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is why the scheme comprises a listing grant and research-related grants to improve the equity research ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Applicants for the research grant are also required to provide coverage for small and mid-cap listed enterprises.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I am sure different agencies will monitor the effectiveness, take in further feedback and inputs and try to improve the scheme over time in order to serve its objectives.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked about corporate governance and whether it should just be left as an internally driven process, and whether SGX RegCo, ACRA can do more.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: He called for an independent task force to review the corporate governance framework and a Government agency to provide oversight on corporate governance standards and improve audit quality.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Actually, many of these features already exist within our current system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS, as the statutory regulator of Singapore's capital markets, and SGX, as the frontline securities market regulator, oversee the corporate governance standards of listed companies, set out in the Code of Corporate Governance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The SGX Listing Rules, in turn, require companies to disclose how the companies' practices conform to the principles in the Code.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: ACRA is responsible for upholding financial reporting and audit quality by inspecting the statutory audits performed by public accountants.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As for an independent task force to review the corporate governance framework, as Mr Dennis Tan has alluded to, MAS has convened an industry-led Corporate Governance Council in 2017.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS accepted all the recommendations that the Council submitted last year in August.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Consequently, changes were made to the Code and the SGX Listing Rules to implement the recommendations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The CGAC comprises prominent industry leaders with stature and corporate experience to advocate good corporate governance practices.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will identify current and potential risks to the quality of corporate governance in Singapore and advise the regulators on corporate governance issues.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: High standards of corporate governance do help sustain good corporate performance for the long term.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It ensures good systems and structures to evaluate investments, manage risks, safeguard all shareholders’ interests, conduct leadership succession and other key processes in the company.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One of the key aims of regulation is to require that investors have access to up-to-date material information, such as a listed company’s financial condition and prospects, in order to make informed investment decisions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Investors, on their part, also need to pay close attention to what is disclosed, look beyond potential returns and assess if they can also accept the risks that come with specific investments.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The regulators, namely, ACRA, MAS, SGX RegCo, will continue to calibrate rules and work with stakeholders, such as the new CGAC, to strengthen the corporate governance standards and practices in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the same time, we will continue to educate the investing public on the tradeoffs between risks and returns, through the MoneySENSE programme.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Lastly, Ms Anthea Ong asked about sustainable financing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS is committed to advance the agenda for sustainable finance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a member of the Network for Greening the Financial System, MAS works closely with our international counterparts to develop best practices for financial institutions to manage climate risks and opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, our local banks have implemented policies aligned with the Guidelines on Responsible Financing issued by the Association of Banks in Singapore, to evaluate their borrowers’ environmental, social and governance (ESG) risks, and help borrowers improve their sustainability profiles.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In this regard, the local banks have also committed to stop new financing of inefficient coal plants.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS also expects insurers to consider environmental risks in their risk assessments and has introduced a climate scenario in our industry-wide stress tests.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, the financial industry is promoting green financing, such as green bonds.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The Minister has prepared a good discussion on all the different initiatives by the National Population and Talent Division.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Mr Vikram Nair for his question.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I could not help but overhear my colleagues' chuckle.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, I have been studying this for some years and perhaps, if Members allow, I could share my own reflection on this.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When we think of births, we think of TFR.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: My observation and my reflection would be that there are really two key sets of driving forces.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One key set of driving forces is longer term in nature.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Births, when looked at from a longer-term perspective, really have to do with values and social norms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And these would include attitudes towards singlehood versus marriage, couplehood versus parenthood.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And then within parenthood, the role played by fathers versus mothers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It would also include norms as to how many children is considered ideal in any society.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And also how people prioritise parenthood versus other pursuits, such as career, caring for elders, service to the community and, very importantly of course, personal lifestyle interests.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Parenting norms also matter a great deal, such as whether, like in the Scandinavian countries, it tends to be quite a relaxed attitude; or whether in an East Asian context, generally a very intensive form of parenting.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These impact costs – how much people spend on children and, of course, as a result the perception of affordability.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And then, as a result, for the parents, how many children they will eventually actually have because of how much they think they can afford.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, these are the longer-term driving forces, a whole set of forces at play.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But in the shorter term, births can also be affected by other things.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, if the job situation is not clear, people are anxious.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Then, you could see that translates into a dip, as what Korea experienced in the last couple of years.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And in fact, one of the "stars", if we could put it that way, of high births, Finland, often touted.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And if we look at the TFR by rural areas versus city areas, actually it is quite across the board.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In Finland's rural as well as city areas, births have declined.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think it has something to do with the sense of malaise and people feeling not confident.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, that is one type of short-term effects, if you could put it that way.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There is also another factor in the short term how TFR could fluctuate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Because TFR is a ratio, so it depends on what you have in the numerator and what you have in the denominator.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I will not go too much into that.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But I would say that these are short-term factors because when confidence returns, it is entirely possible that people who have put off parenthood in Finland could then decide that this is the time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And then you might see an uptick in their TFR.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, the long-term factors versus the shorter-term factors.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What would be important for us is really not to be overly distracted by the year-to-year ups and downs in TFR.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We pay attention to them, we look at them, and we ask ourselves why it is happening this way.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But do not be overly focused on it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What we should really focus on would be the values and our societal norms, which many Members spoke about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is important for us to firstly remember we have to strengthen the fundamentals.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Those are the things we have to focus on.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In one of my cuts on public sector transformation, I asked the Minister, in our drive towards upskilling and reskilling in the Public Service, whether the Public Service can partner the Labour Movement as well as the public sector unions in forming training committees to drive some of these training efforts that cross our Ministries and Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Chairman, that is definitely a good suggestion.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As the former immediate past Secretary-General of NTUC, I would certainly take note of that.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I would say that we are not setting up a big overall committee to integrate with the Amalgamated Union of Public Employees (AUPE) at that level, but importantly, we are starting at the respective job levels.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, for example, there are lower-skilled workers in the Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources (MEWR) who require new skillsets and we are focusing our attention on them, prioritising them in our transformation effort first.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Likewise, the CSC will also contact and work closely with the Labour Movement to make sure that the modular system of training is made available to as many of the public servants as possible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We welcome this move by the Labour Movement and the offer by the Labour Movement and will certainly work closely with AUPE to bring this about.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Mr Chairman, I have a clarification for Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary on my cut on personal data protection in the public agencies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I would like a clarification from him as to whether it is the expressed Government policy that persons whose data has been compromised, while in the care of public agencies, that such persons have a right to know that there has been a breach and that they have the right to know in a timely manner.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Chairman, we addressed some of these in the discussion recently in the previous Sitting.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are guidelines about how public sector officials should handle the matter of a data breach involving citizens' particulars.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do need to look at every case, and we do need to look at the issue at hand as to what has been accessed, what are the circumstances, what the potential impact would be on the citizen to be involved in that process thereafter.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are guidelines about how the matter should be handled.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are guidelines about how citizens should be approached.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The situation needs to be taken on a case-by-case basis and all the factors that are relevant need to be taken into account.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Mr Chairman, can I kindly request for Minister Chan to further expand on my question on how or what specific measures or steps is the Government taking to restore confidence in the Public Service?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Chairman, every time when something goes wrong in the Public Service, regardless of which agency, the first thing to do is to get to the bottom of it by the respective agency to see what are the lessons learnt that the agencies must do internally to make sure that they get to the bottom of it and put things right.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second step that we always will do is to make sure that these lessons are shared across all the other agencies because things that happen in one agency can offer important lessons to other agencies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There is a third step that I would always ask the Public Service to do, which is that when we do our debrief, to ask ourselves if we could have prevented or pre-empted this incident right at the beginning.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And that is why I always discuss and share with my fellow colleagues in the Public Service that it is necessary but not sufficient just to put things right.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Actually, more important than playing defensive, we need to make sure that our systems are in place to pre-empt problems from arising in the first place.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Of course, it is very difficult for the Public Service to say that I have done this and, therefore, I have prevented these problems because the problems never even manifest themselves.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is the high benchmark that we need to set for ourselves as the Singapore Public Service if we aspire to be a Public Service that Singapore and Singaporeans can be proud of.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And, indeed, as I shared, we have done many things that I think we can be proud of because that has put Singapore at the forefront of many of these views so that we have prevented and pre-empted many of these issues.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Be that as it may, we should never be complacent.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, the way to restore public confidence is to make sure, one, we get to the bottom of the issue; and if there are people who are responsible, we will make sure that we rectify that; even as we take the responsibility at that level, we would ask ourselves could we have trained that person better, could we have changed our process to take into account the human factors to prevent those mistakes from happening in the first place?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, these are things that we owe it to ourselves in the Public Service to get things right and to prevent things from going wrong in the first place because it gives us no joy to say that we are able to recover from our mistakes fast.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Could I just ask what percentage do not have this single structure scheme and what are we doing to close this gap?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But my cut really was about how are we going to ensure that they do and whether we can have internal QSMs to take that role instead, to take that feedback given, it is actually looked into and the loop is closed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Could I ask whether the entire Public Service can offer this unpaid leave for parents with multiple or preterm babies so that we can walk the talk and we can take the lead on this issue?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Lastly, with regard to childcare leave, could I ask the Minister to consider again whether we can allow people to use their current sick leave entitlements, not just when they are sick, but again when their children are sick and, to avoid people from misusing this, they have to provide the child's MC as proof when they take this kind of sick leave?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Chairman, let me first clarify that our aim is not to merge every scheme possible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: You cannot do that because there are schemes that are for professionals – doctors, engineers, accountants.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, our aim in the Public Service is not to merge every scheme.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Now, even for those who have done so, we will constantly challenge ourselves.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Are we able to merge those schemes even earlier, at an earlier stage whereby we take into account an individual's performance rather than just the academic grades?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, going forward, we will see the following things.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Yes, academic grades will be taken into account as one of the signs as a proxy of what the person is capable of, but increasingly, as I mentioned, there will be other skillsets that we are required to take into account for a holistic assessment of the individual.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To what extent we can, I think beyond those professional schemes and engineers, qualified engineers and doctors, we will try to that extent possible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Member's second question is about how do the leaders follow up on their respective agencies when they get the feedback?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, when they get the feedback, I expect them to take actions on their own.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And, of course, all the respective agencies' feedback comes to me and, if necessary, I will have a discussion with the respective Permanent Secretaries or the Chief Executives of the various agencies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They know that we take this seriously, they know that I expect them to take this seriously and, if need be, I will let them know.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But if the Member knows of any which somehow is not in that list of 70, feel free to let me know.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On the question on whether parents' leave entitlements can be used for their children, here I want to just have a word of caution.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I remember some years ago when I was still in the Labour Movement, NPTD at that time was doing consultation on whether we should raise the Maternity Leave benefits.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, it surprised me, but when we did the engagement with our women unionists, they were very wise and they said to me, "Sister, be careful about what we ask for because whenever we increase these leave benefits, we look different to the employers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They start seeing us differently, because they start seeing us in terms of the liability and obligations that they have towards us." So, not all of them were so keen to expand the leave benefits.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, that was a very useful exercise and I keep bearing it in mind.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What the Member has asked for, I think amounts to that; you are really going to expand the leave provisions for people who are parents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Not that you cannot do that, but, by doing so, we have to ask ourselves what the employers will think of it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: From having obligations to the individual as an employee, now they have obligations to the entire family.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The same benefits can extend to the whole family.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And I will be very careful about this because, primarily, the leave provisions were designed to protect the individual in the event of illness.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If we think that society can bear more leave provisions for those who are going to be parents, I think we do it openly, we do it in a transparent fashion, we do it in a way that is honest with the employers so that they do not have to second-guess when they take on an employee whether there are these other hidden obligations that they have to fulfil.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: For Minister Chan Chun Sing, just one clarification and one suggestion.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: When the Minister earlier mentioned about public sector transformation, he will have his officer work with AUPE to ensure that public sector servants are assisted and well-coached as far as training is concerned.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: I think the Minister also referred to the Statutory Board unions and those who are House unions, not just those that are belonging to AUPE, just for clarification, so that the other union leaders and members will not feel left out that their areas are not looked after.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: I had a conversation with many of them and they have mentioned that a lot of the trainings are centred on the workers themselves – on the lower-skilled or the older ones.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: Then, they realised that their supervisor could be much younger, could be somebody who is in their 30s or 20s.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: And they realised that, sometimes, the supervisors do not quite understand that this transition, this situation that they face, require some level of empathy, some assistance and some mentoring and coaching from the supervisors.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: So, the suggestion is that, can supervisors that oversee some of these workers also go through a system of training whereby they are able to coach and guide these officers along so that the entire transformation and the ability to adapt will be something that is owned by both the staff as well as the supervisors and, therefore, make the workplace more inclusive?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Mr Ang Hin Kee for reminding me to clarify this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, that it is at the respective agencies' level because we find through our experience that the most impactful training is when it is focused on the respective agencies rather than the generic skillsets.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But there is also a place for very focused, targeted intervention at the respective agencies' level.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But the Member is right that we also have other forms of training that include the intermediate managers and even the higher managers because different levels of managers require different skillsets.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, in the Member's particular situation, indeed, for the middle managers, they must know how to make use of some of these technologies; besides using it, how to exploit this technology, how to use, how to help their fellow workers to adopt and adapt to such technologies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Yet, at the higher level, at the more senior management level, we expect them not to just be hands on, but also to know the potential to use some of these new technologies to restructure and change the processes which they are doing at their job at the current point in time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, Members can see that in this overall digital masterplan or the digital skills masterplan, we are looking at different skillsets for different managers at different levels.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, that is, indeed, what we are going to do at the training at CSC as they roll out across the Civil Service.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I would just like to encourage Members, you have been doing well in time-keeping.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We get to go home earlier than expected, it might help our TFR as well.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We will check back on next year's Budget.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Patrick Tay, do you wish to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to thank the responses from Minister Chan Chun Sing on building a great Public Service; Minister Josephine Teo for sharing on how we are going to support families, parenthood and marriage; Minister Dr Vivian Balakrishnan and Senior Minister of State Dr Janil Puthucheary on not just building a smarter nation, but really one on improving lives and livelihoods; Minister Ong Ye Kung on strengthening our financial markets and our regulatory system; Head (Civil Service) and the PSD team, as well as all our public servants, for putting us all at the heart of what they do and working hard to ensure we are top-notch and first-class.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: On that note, I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
